questions.text: Why does Q-learning use max over next-state action values while SARSA uses the value of the action actually selected next?

options.A: Q-learning estimates the greedy target policy; SARSA evaluates the behavior policy that still explores.
options.B: Q-learning requires known transitions; SARSA estimates transitions from sampled episodes.
options.C: Q-learning removes discounting; SARSA discounts rewards according to the chosen action.
options.D: Q-learning averages all actions; SARSA selects the action with highest estimated value.

questions.explanation: Q-learning bootstraps toward the greedy next action even while behavior explores; SARSA bootstraps from the next action actually chosen by its current policy.

questions.text: During training on cliff walking, exploration sometimes steps into the cliff. You want learned values to account for that continuing exploration risk. Which update should you choose?

options.A: Q-learning, because its max target includes the random action taken next.
options.B: SARSA, because its target uses the next action selected by the exploring policy.
options.C: Q-learning, because it replaces sampled rewards with known transition probabilities.
options.D: SARSA, because it ignores future action values when a cliff is nearby.

questions.explanation: SARSA bootstraps from the action actually selected under the exploring policy, so its values reflect occasional exploratory cliff falls.

questions.text: A nonterminal Q-learning update has Q(s,a)=2, reward r=1, γ=0.5, α=0.25, and next-state action values [4, 0]. What is the updated Q(s,a)?
questions.explanation: The target is 1 + 0.5×max(4,0) = 3. The update is 2 + 0.25×(3−2) = 2.25.
